topic: Unique Pointer: Stateless Deleter Zero-Size Optimization
explanation:
The unique pointer is the primary smart pointer in modern C++ for managing resources with a single, unambiguous owner. It embodies the concept of exclusive ownership, meaning that at any given time, only one unique pointer can own the resource. This makes it a lightweight, highly efficient, and safe alternative to raw pointers for most ownership scenarios.

Scott Meyers emphasizes that the unique pointer should be your default choice for a smart pointer. His critical insight is that it is a zero-overhead abstraction. In its most common configuration (without a custom deleter), a unique pointer is the same size as a raw pointer and its operations, including dereferencing, compile down to the same machine instructions. This means there is no performance penalty for the safety and convenience it provides, making it suitable even in resource-constrained or high-performance environments where developers might have previously felt compelled to use raw pointers.

Its ownership semantics are enforced at compile time through its move-only nature. A unique pointer cannot be copied; attempting to do so will result in a compilation error. This design choice is fundamental, as it prevents the common bug of multiple pointers owning and attempting to delete the same resource. Ownership can only be transferred from one unique pointer to another through an explicit move operation. When the unique pointer that currently owns the resource is destroyed—either by going out of scope, being reset, or having a new pointer moved into it—its destructor automatically deallocates the managed resource. This provides a strong RAII guarantee for exclusive ownership.

In practice, unique pointers are the ideal tool for several common patterns. They are perfect for returning a heap-allocated object from a factory function, as the caller receives unambiguous ownership of the newly created object. They are also excellent for implementing the Pimpl (Pointer to Implementation) idiom, where a class member exclusively owns its implementation object, effectively hiding implementation details and improving compilation times. By making unique pointers the default for class members that are pointers, you ensure that resources are automatically cleaned up with the parent object, simplifying destructors and preventing leaks in complex class hierarchies.

The primary trade-off is its inherent exclusivity. If a resource needs to be shared among multiple owners with an indeterminate lifetime, a unique pointer is not the right tool; a shared pointer is required. A potential gotcha involves custom deleters. While unique pointers support custom deleters for managing non-memory resources, a stateful deleter (such as a lambda with captures or a function object with member variables) will increase the size of the unique pointer, nullifying the zero-size-overhead benefit. However, stateless deleters, like free functions or captureless lambdas, do not add any size overhead.
practical_example: A `Document` class in a word processor might exclusively own a large, heap-allocated `TextBuffer` object. By using a unique pointer for the `TextBuffer` member, the `Document`'s destructor doesn't need to manually delete the buffer. When a `Document` object is destroyed, the unique pointer automatically handles the cleanup of its `TextBuffer`, ensuring no memory leaks. If the document is moved, ownership of the buffer is efficiently transferred along with it.
